verdict_reasoning: The decisive objection is replication-ondisk-1. The flat table needs slot x unlinked before it is reused, message #12 rejects the spinlock-held delete that guarantees this, and no posted version carries an agreed replacement. maintenance-fit-1 adds that no check catches a later path that breaks the rule. demand-1 and prior-attempts-1 are open but do not stop the idea, since message #2 supports a separate table and the micro-benchmarks and memory saving are real.

brief.title: Replace dynahash with a flat, array-based shared buffer lookup table
brief.problem: The shared buffer mapping table uses dynahash, whose directory, segment, bucket-chain and freelist layers the author calls excessive for this one table. Each buffer hit, insert and eviction pays that cost, and the table uses more memory than needed. The target is every workload with heavy buffer lookups, and large buffer pools in particular.
brief.proposed_design: buf_table.c gets its own table built on two arrays: bucket heads and entries, with entries[x] always describing buffer x. Each entry holds a BufferTag and a next index, so each bucket is a linked list over the flat arrays. Because a slot cannot hold a stale and a new entry at once, the patch moves BufTableDelete() under the buffer header spinlock in InvalidateBuffer().
user_visible_surface: Shared memory allocation "Shared Buffer Lookup Table" in pg_shmem_allocations is replaced by "Shared Buffer Lookup Buckets" and "Shared Buffer Lookup Entries".
BufTableInsert/BufTableLookup/BufTableDelete keep their role; reviewer variants add delete by buffer id.
Benchmark test module buftable_bench with SQL functions buftable_bench_probe() and buftable_bench_collide(); x86_64 only.
author_claims: Micro-benchmarks show lookup, insert and delete about 1.2 to 2.2 times faster than dynahash at 256MB to 16GB shared_buffers.
Gains shrink at 16GB in the first message's test; the author links this to cache behaviour at larger sizes.
At 128MB the table uses about half the shared memory of dynahash (Heikki's measurement).
pgbench shows no statistically significant TPS change, with small select-only gains (author's 30-run rerun).
A follow-up design resizes the table online with linear hashing, for the dynamic shared buffers work.
brief.thread_state: Heikki, Andres, Andrey Borodin and reviewer Alexandre Felipe replied; Andres rejects holding the header spinlock across BufTableDelete() and doubts the value next to a radix-tree redesign. Alexandre posted v6 with two-step delete and dropped his lock-free variant after CFBot failed in 027_stream_regress; no fixed author version is posted.
unclear: The material does not show which patch version is the one under review: Dhruv's v1 or Alexandre's v6.
No final fix is agreed for the slot-reuse race without holding the spinlock during delete.
No real workload shows a measurable end-to-end gain; Andrey saw a possible simple-update regression.
The proposal does not say how this table fits with the dynamic shared buffers patch it depends on for resizing.
Andres's architectural concerns (per-relation iteration, ordered lookup, 20-byte keys) get no answer on whether this blocks them.

prior_attempts.title: drop/truncate table sucks for large values of shared buffers
prior_attempts.quote: Committing a band-aid will just make it harder to pursue real fixes.
prior_attempts.reason: Tom Lane objected that the approach fails badly if the caller is wrong about the relation's maximum page number (for example, kernel lseek bugs). He also noted that it does not help DROP TABLESPACE or DROP DATABASE, which also scan the whole buffer pool. Heikki Linnakangas returned it with feedback, citing the issues raised, a still-unwritten alternative (delayed cleanup during the checkpoint scan), and a preference for a structure such as a radix tree that can find all buffers for a relation or database. Tom Lane added that committing a band-aid would make more complete fixes harder to pursue.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P3 added a per-block lookup path for DROP/TRUNCATE, and this proposal replaces the table for every lookup. P3's reasons concern that path and do not transfer; the shared point is the stated preference for a radix-tree structure.

objections.title: Slot-reuse invariant has no agreed safe design, and a miss means duplicate buffers
objections.failure_scenario: InvalidateBuffer() releases buffer x, and a concurrent backend reuses slot x before the old entry is unlinked. The bucket chain breaks, so a later BufTableLookup() misses a block that is still cached. A second buffer is then loaded for the same page, one copy's changes are lost at write-out, and the loss shows up only later as heap or index corruption, on a primary or during standby replay.
objections.argument: Because entries[x] must describe buffer x, a stale entry and a new entry cannot exist at the same time (message #16). The v1 fix holds the buffer header spinlock across BufTableDelete(). Andres rejects that in message #12, since an error there cannot be recovered and it risks deadlock with the partition lock. The v6 two-step delete (message #18) comes with no argument for why the invariant holds, and the CFBot failures in 027_stream_regress (message #24) show that this test does catch races in this table.
objections.author_must_show: Without the spinlock held across BufTableDelete(), what ordering of buffer header lock and partition lock stops slot x from being reused before its old entry is unlinked, including when an error is raised partway?

precedents.title: BufferAlloc: don't take two simultaneous locks

critic.reasoning: Message #16 confirms the flat table is unsafe without the spinlock-held delete, which message #12 rejects, and no posted version carries an agreed replacement. [P7] closed for lack of a rebase and must not be used as support; the CFBot failure concerned the withdrawn lock-free variant.

objections.title: Slot-reuse invariant adds a silent rule for every buffer-reuse path
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch adds a new path that evicts or reuses a buffer, for example shrinking shared buffers online, and releases the header lock before the mapping delete. A concurrent backend reuses slot x and cuts the old chain, so lookups miss cached pages and the same page can be read into a second buffer. Nothing asserts, and the damage shows up later as corruption.
objections.argument: Dynahash tolerates a stale entry and a new entry at once because it allocates from a freelist (message #16), but the flat table does not. v1 closes the race by holding the header spinlock across BufTableDelete(), which message #12 rejects as unsafe, since spinlocks have no error recovery and the change risks deadlock. The lock-free variant failed 027_stream_regress on CFBot (message #24) and was withdrawn (message #25). No posted version states the replacement protocol or how a violation would be detected.
objections.author_must_show: What protocol replaces the spinlock-held delete, and what check makes a future reuse path fail loudly if it breaks the entries[x] invariant?

critic.reasoning: This is distinct from replication-ondisk-1 because it concerns future buffer-reuse paths, such as the shared buffers shrink planned in message #7. The thread states no protocol, and no check that fails when a new path breaks the entries[x] invariant.

objections.title: No workload-level gain shown to justify a dedicated hash table
objections.failure_scenario: A committer pushes a custom buffer mapping table on micro-benchmark numbers. Users running pgbench-like or production workloads see no TPS change, but every later bufmgr patch has to respect the new slot-reuse invariant. The project finds out when a buffer-mapping redesign has to replace or work around it.
objections.argument: The only end-to-end data shows no significant TPS change: the author's 30-run rerun has confidence intervals spanning zero in most cells (message #10), and Andrey saw a possible simple-update regression (message #9). The brief targets large buffer pools, but the speedup shrinks to about 1.02x for insert and delete at 16GB (message #1, message #27). Heikki asked for real-world impact (message #2), and no field report or profile with numbers has answered it. Andres questions spending review bandwidth here instead of on the architectural problems (message #12).
objections.author_must_show: Which real workload, at which shared_buffers size, spends measurable CPU in BufTableLookup today and shows a repeatable end-to-end gain with this patch?

precedents.title: drop/truncate table sucks for large values of shared buffers

critic.reasoning: Heikki asked for real-world impact in message #2, and the pgbench runs in messages #9 and #10 show no significant change. The 1.02x figure at 16GB is contradicted by the later probe results (1.3 to 1.9 times), and [P3] does not bear on demand.

objections.title: Tuning the hash table may delay the buffer mapping redesign
objections.failure_scenario: The flat table is committed, and the linear-hashing resize from message #7 is then built on it for dynamic shared buffers. Later, someone starts the relation-plus-block radix tree from message #12 and finds two hash-specific layers to replace. The constraint that entries[x] describes buffer x now ties bufmgr.c to the old layout.
objections.argument: [P3] was returned partly because a band-aid was seen to make a structure that finds all buffers of a relation harder to pursue. Andres repeats that point here in message #12: per-relation iteration, ordered lookup and 20-byte keys, plus doubt about spending effort on the current design. Message #25 answers with cost estimates for a radix tree, but the thread did not settle the point. The proposal does not say whether the flat table is a step toward the redesign or a separate path.
objections.author_must_show: Does the flat table, with its planned resize, make the per-relation, ordered buffer mapping in message #12 any easier or harder to build later?

precedents.title: drop/truncate table sucks for large values of shared buffers

critic.reasoning: Andres raises this in message #12 and the author does not answer it; message #25 only gives a reviewer's cost estimates. [P3] concerned a DROP/TRUNCATE lookup path, so it must not be used as support, and an internal table can be replaced later.

refuted.title: Bespoke table optimizes a design that a radix redesign would replace
refuted.failure_scenario: The project commits a custom hash table in buf_table.c, with resize logic to follow in buf_resize.c. A later two-layer design with per-relation and ordered lookup (message #12) must replace both and redo the invalidation protocol. Until then, DROP and TRUNCATE still scan all of shared buffers.
refuted.argument: End-to-end, the author's 30-run pgbench shows no significant TPS change (message #10), and message #9 reports small select-only gains and a possible simple-update regression. Message #12 doubts the value of making the current design faster when the same effort could go to its architectural problems, but Heikki supports a separate implementation (message #2). [P3] was returned partly because a structure that can find all buffers for a relation was preferred, with the note that a band-aid makes real fixes harder.
refuted.author_must_show: Which parts of this table carry over into a per-relation, ordered lookup design, and which real workload gains enough to justify maintaining it until then?

precedents_retrieved.title: Map WAL segment files on PMEM as WAL buffers
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patchset maps WAL segment files that live on persistent memory (PMEM) directly into memory with libpmem and uses them as the WAL buffers, so WAL is written in place without a separate copy and write. It adds a --with-libpmem build option and a wal_pmem_map setting, and sizes the mapped buffers to min_wal_size with pre-allocation by walwriter.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer took it up. Jacob Champion returned it in a batch of patchsets that did not get enough reviewer interest, and he wrote that this was not a rejection and that there was little actionable feedback. Earlier messages only asked for build fixes, CI support and rebases, and the author did each of them.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As discussed in [1], we're taking this opportunity to return some
patchsets that don't appear to be getting enough reviewer interest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Detect shared buffer access violations using mprotect()
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a compile-time option (-DMPROTECT_BUFFER) that uses mprotect() to mark shared buffers read-only or read-write according to pin and content-lock state, so that violations of shared buffer access rules are caught. The patch came out of a discussion of places that modify shared buffers without holding the content lock.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane asked that the patch be restructured so that bad accesses can be caught with either Valgrind or mprotect depending on compile options, using macros such as ProtectBuffer() that expand to nothing when the feature is disabled instead of inline #ifdef blocks. He also raised the concern that buffers are not reliably aligned on system page boundaries. The author did not address this feedback before the commitfest ended, so Andres Freund marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It'd be better to
set things up so that the patch adds support for catching bad accesses
with either valgrind or mprotect, according to compile options.

precedents_retrieved.title: Auto-tune shared_buffers to use available huge pages
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a setting (first huge_pages_autotune_buffers, later shared_buffers_autotune_target) that makes Postgres raise shared_buffers at startup until the shared memory request reaches a target size, such as the huge pages given to a Kubernetes pod. It moves the existing auto-tuning of other settings into dedicated functions so they use the configured shared_buffers, and adds a checkpoint_request_size GUC.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Ashutosh Bapat asked whether a script that finds the right shared_buffers with postgres -C is enough. The author replied that such a script must run before every start, which Docker images, Patroni and operators do not easily allow, and the thread had no further replies before the entry was withdrawn.

precedents_retrieved.title: BufferAlloc: don't take two simultaneous locks
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes BufferAlloc so that, when it evicts a valid buffer, it releases the old buffer-mapping partition lock before it takes the new one, so it never holds two partition locks at once. Later versions also let dynahash reuse the evicted entry, and a v12 variant inserts a placeholder entry and makes concurrent inserters of the same block wait on a per-backend ConditionVariable.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback after the patch stopped applying and the author did not rebase it after the September 2022 notice. Earlier, Robert Haas objected to the HASH_REUSE design, which splits one dynahash operation across bufmgr and dynahash, so an ereport(ERROR) between HASH_REUSE and HASH_ENTER would corrupt state. He suggested a hash_replace() call, but the author rejected it because it would need both partition locks.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
With no rebase done since this notice, I have marked this entry as
RwF.

precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an OldestInitializedPage field to XLogCtl that tracks the start address of the oldest initialized WAL buffer page, updated under WALBufMappingLock. precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts 06c418e163, e37662f221, bf1e650806, 25f42429e2,
ee79928441, and 74eaf66f98 per review by Heikki Linnakangas.

roaster_notes.note: Only [P3] carries a reason that still applies. The [P7] reason is a missing rebase.

The user-facing contract barely changes: no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog, dump or psql change. The only visible change, the split of the "Shared Buffer Lookup Table" row in pg_shmem_allocations into two rows, follows how shared memory allocation names already change between releases, and a committer would not block on it. The objections that matter here are about locking safety and design, which other angles cover.

The proposal changes only shared-memory structures. It touches no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol or pg_upgrade path. The only exposed name change is in pg_shmem_allocations. My one objection is about an in-memory invariant whose failure leads to lost page writes.

The proposal changes an internal shared memory structure and adds no privilege, role, SQL surface or new data exposure. A collision-based denial of service would need control over relfilenumbers, and dynahash has the same exposure, so I found no realistic failure scenario. The spinlock and error-recovery risks belong to the safety and design angle, and Andres raised them in message #12.
Two objections from the maintenance angle. Hot-path cost for non-users is not a concern, since the change targets the lookup path for everyone and the measurements show it is faster.

No existing feature meets this need, so this angle raises nothing. The closest alternative is removing the directory indirection from dynahash for all shmem hash tables (message #2), but Heikki himself judged a separate table for buffer lookup worthwhile. A generic dynahash change also could not provide the entries[x]-is-buffer-x layout or the memory saving. No extension can replace buf_table.c, and radixtree.h belongs to the redesign Andres proposed (message #12), which is a design question for other angles.
Interest in a faster buffer lookup is real: Heikki and Andres both call dynahash a poor fit here. What is missing is evidence of a workload-level benefit.
